title: Buffett's 2024 letter: mistakes, Pete Liegl, float, and why Berkshire stays in equities
summary: Buffett's 2024 annual letter covers owning up to capital allocation and personnel mistakes, judging managers by character rather than schooling, the discipline of P/C insurance and float, and Berkshire's permanent preference for businesses over cash. It also celebrates 60 years of reinvestment, which produced record tax payments.

principles.text: Admit mistakes openly and correct them fast; delay is the cardinal sin.
principles.quote: The cardinal sin is delaying the correction of mistakes or what Charlie Munger called “thumb-sucking.” Problems, he would tell me, cannot be wished away. They require action, however uncomfortable that may be.

principles.text: One great decision outweighs many mistakes; winners compound while losses fade.
principles.quote: a single winning decision can make a breathtaking difference over time. (Think GEICO as a business decision, Ajit Jain as a managerial decision and my luck in finding Charlie Munger as a one-of-a-kind partner, personal advisor and steadfast friend.) Mistakes fade away; winners can forever blossom.

principles.text: Judge managers on innate ability and character, not pedigree or schooling.
principles.quote: One further point in our CEO selections: I never look at where a candidate has gone to school. Never!

principles.text: Never write underpriced insurance to stay in the game; underwriters should be nervous but not paralyzed.
principles.quote: We must never write inadequately-priced policies in order to stay in the game. That policy is corporate suicide.

principles.text: Keep skin in the game; avoid one-sided compensation so managers share downside.
principles.quote: We do not use options or other one-sided forms of compensation; if you lose money, so do we. This approach encourages caution but does not ensure foresight.

principles.text: Hold the majority of capital in good businesses, not cash or fixed-coupon bonds, to guard against currency debasement.
principles.quote: Berkshire will never prefer ownership of cash-equivalent assets over the ownership of good businesses, whether controlled or only partially owned.
